cachyos/optimized-repositories-and-x86-6.title: Optimized Repositories and x86-64 Levels
cachyos/optimized-repositories-and-x86-6.content:
Part of CachyOS Wiki Notes. From the official CachyOS wiki (last updated 2026-06-14).
Optimized Repositories and x86-64 Levels
CachyOS recompiles Arch packages for x86-64-v3, x86-64-v4, and Zen4+.


x86-64-v3: 5–20% performance uplift over baseline x86-64.


x86-64-v4: substantial gains via AVX512, workload-dependent.


Zen 4/5: v4 plus extra instructions:
abm, adx, aes, avx512bf16, avx512bitalg, avx512ifma, avx512vbmi, avx512vbmi2, avx512vnni,avx512vpopctndq, clflushopt, clwb, clzero, fsgsbase, gfni, mwaitx, pclmul, pku, prfchw,rpdid, rdrnd, rdseed, sha, sse4a, vaes, vockmulqdq, wbnoinvd, savec, xsaveopt, xsaves



Customized packages
The CachyOS-PKGBUILDs repo carries packages with ongoing updates, patches and backported fixes. Selective PGO, LTO and BOLT optimizations; some -git packages are maintained (e.g. mesa-git). Search at packages.cachyos.org/ (shows compilation architecture, last update date, etc.).
Migrating x86-64-v3 → x86-64-v4 or znver4

Trap: Intel 12th gen (Alder Lake) and newer may report x86-64-v4 but cannot run AVX-512 — P-cores support it, E-cores do not, which causes instability. Intel disabled it via microcode/BIOS updates (early chips; re-enable only by avoiding/rolling back microcode) and by hardware fusing (2022+ chips, permanent). Treat these CPUs as x86-64-v3 only.

Verify v4 support:
/lib/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 --help | grep supported
A x86-64-v4 (supported, searched) line means supported; no v4 line means unsupported. Example:
$ /lib/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 --help | grep supported
  x86-64-v2 (supported, searched)
  x86-64-v3 (supported, searched)
  x86-64-v4 (supported, searched)

For AMD Zen 4/5, check the reported arch:
gcc -march=native -Q --help=target 2>&1 | grep -Po "^\s+-march=\s+\K(\w+)$"
Output znver4 or znver5 means you can migrate. Both x86-64-v4 and znver4 use the same mirrorlist: /etc/pacman.d/cachyos-v4-mirrorlist.
Migration steps:


Edit /etc/pacman.conf, replacing the x86-64-v3 repos. Keep [cachyos], [core], [extra], [multilib] unchanged:
[cachyos-v4]
Include = /etc/pacman.d/cachyos-v4-mirrorlist
 
[cachyos-core-v4]
Include = /etc/pacman.d/cachyos-v4-mirrorlist
 
[cachyos-extra-v4]
Include = /etc/pacman.d/cachyos-v4-mirrorlist


Clear cache and sync DBs:
sudo pacman -Scc   # Confirm with 'y' twice
sudo pacman -Sy


Reinstall everything to switch architecture:
pacman -Qqn | sudo pacman -S -


Reboot.


Adding these repos to an existing Arch install
Check the CPU compatibility list in Preparing a CachyOS USB Installer first. Then the automated script (detects CPU instruction sets, installs the most optimized repos, backs up the old pacman.conf):
curl mirror.cachyos.org/cachyos-repo.tar.xz -o cachyos-repo.tar.xz
tar xvf cachyos-repo.tar.xz && cd cachyos-repo
sudo ./cachyos-repo.sh
Uninstalling the repos
curl mirror.cachyos.org/cachyos-repo.tar.xz -o cachyos-repo.tar.xz
tar xvf cachyos-repo.tar.xz
cd cachyos-repo
sudo ./cachyos-repo.sh --remove
Benchmarks
Phoronix (Michael Larabel) has benchmarked CachyOS repeatedly since 2022 — including an Arch x86_64-v2 RFC (2021), “The Performance Of Arch Linux Powered CachyOS” (2022-09-12), “Arch Linux CachyOS Benchmarks Of x86-64-v3 & x86-64-v4 Repositories” (2024-02-29), and a Ryzen 9 9950X OS comparison (2024-08-20). Caveat noted on the page: Liquid-DSP and RocksDB were compiled by the Phoronix suite ignoring /etc/makepkg.conf flags, giving unexpected CachyOS results.

cachyos/post-install-setup.title: Post Install Setup
cachyos/post-install-setup.content:
Part of CachyOS Wiki Notes. From the official CachyOS wiki (last updated 2026-08-27). Recommended steps, in order.
1. Update the system
Options: Shelly (GUI & CLI), Octopi (GUI), Pacman, Offline System Update, Cachy-Update.


Shelly CLI: shelly, shelly install --upgrade {pkg}, shelly remove {pkg}, shelly aur search {pkg}.


Pacman:
sudo pacman -Syu


Offline updates via pacman-offline:
sudo pacman -S pacman-offline
Add Include = /etc/pacman.d/offline.conf to /etc/pacman.conf after the [options] section, then fill /etc/pacman.d/offline.conf with IgnorePkg = lines for the Arch and CachyOS kernels. Run once with sudo systemctl start pacman-offline-prepare.service; automate with sudo systemctl enable pacman-offline-prepare.timer and optionally pacman-offline-reboot.timer (reboots by default at 3am with a 2h randomized delay).


Cachy-Update (fork of Arch-Update) — enable/disable in CachyOS Hello > Apps/Tweaks. Checks once two minutes after boot, then once a day with a one hour random delay. Timer override: systemctl --user edit --full arch-update.timer; defaults OnStartupSec=2min, RandomizedDelaySec=1h, OnUnitActiveSec=1d. Hide the tray:
mkdir -p ~/.config/autostart
echo -e "[Desktop Entry]\nHidden=true" > ~/.config/autostart/arch-update-tray.desktop
Stop checks: systemctl --user disable --now arch-update.timer. Supports sudo, sudo-rs, doas, run0.


Reboot after a big update, especially a kernel update.


2. Firewall (ufw)

Caution: improperly configured firewall rules can lock you out of your own system. Be careful here.

Enabled by default after installation.
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw disable
sudo ufw allow ssh
sudo ufw allow 12345
sudo ufw deny ssh
sudo ufw deny 12345
sudo ufw status verbose
Default policy: ignore incoming, allow outgoing. Allow/deny changes take effect after ufw is restarted (disable then enable for an immediate effect). Rules can carry comments: sudo ufw allow 12345 comment 'Example'. Also configurable graphically in KDE Plasma’s Firewall settings.
3. Global menu
Some apps (VS Code, for instance) otherwise attach the menu to the parent app.
# To enable global menu support, run the command and restart the app.
sudo pacman -S appmenu-gtk-module libdbusmenu-glib
Optional configurations


Default shell — CachyOS uses fish as the user’s login shell; bash remains root’s. chsh -s /usr/bin/bash or chsh -s /usr/bin/zsh (CachyOS ships a zsh config aiming for 1:1 parity with its fish config).


tldr — CachyOS uses tealdeer, a faster Rust implementation: tldr --update, then e.g. tldr java.


AppImages — chmod +x /path/to/your/appimage; FUSE is required (sudo pacman -S fuse2). Manage them with Gear Lever: sudo pacman -S flatpak, restart, flatpak install flathub it.mijorus.gearlever, then log out/in.


Samba shares — assumes a working Samba server. Back up /etc/samba/smb.conf, install sudo pacman -S cachyos-samba-settings on the client, copy its smb.conf to the server, edit shares, then sudo systemctl restart --now samba. Access via smb://<your_server_ip>/<share_name>.


AppArmor (apparmor.d profiles) — the wiki is explicit: do not proceed without understanding the implications. Add the kernel parameter lsm=landlock,lockdown,yama,integrity,apparmor,bpf in the boot manager; sudo pacman -S apparmor apparmor.d; systemctl enable --now apparmor.service; add write-cache, Optimize=compress-fast, cache-loc /etc/apparmor/earlypolicy/ to /etc/apparmor/parser.conf; save and reboot.


TRIM on encrypted (LUKS) devices — CachyOS enables fstrim.timer by default, but dm-crypt/LUKS blocks discard unless passthrough is explicitly enabled, so periodic TRIM silently does nothing on encrypted partitions. Security caveat: someone with physical access could infer approximate used space, filesystem layout, or data patterns. Find the mapper with lsblk (look for the crypt type entry, e.g. luks-1e647929-...), then:
sudo cryptsetup --allow-discards --persistent refresh <mapper_name>
Reboot and verify:
lsblk -D
sudo fstrim -v /
lsblk -D should show non-zero DISC-GRAN and DISC-MAX, and fstrim prints the amount trimmed.


Related: Btrfs Snapshots, Boot Manager Configuration, CachyOS Settings Package.

cachyos/preparing-a-cachyos-usb-installe.title: Preparing a CachyOS USB Installer
cachyos/preparing-a-cachyos-usb-installe.content:
Part of CachyOS Wiki Notes. From the official CachyOS wiki (last updated 2025-12-03).
Preparing a CachyOS USB Installer
Before you start

Installation is online only — a stable, reasonably fast internet connection is mandatory. Unstable internet means long install times or outright failure.
Not recommended in a VM (broken/incorrect config is possible); bare metal is recommended.
Minimum: 3 GB RAM, 30 GB storage, stable internet.
USB drive: at least 8 GB free.
Keep a copy of the ISO on the drive (or elsewhere) for later troubleshooting via chroot.

x86-64 microarchitecture levels

x86-64-v3 — AMD Family 15h (Excavator), 17h (Zen/Zen+/Zen 2), 19h (Zen 3); Intel 4th Gen (Haswell) through 10th Gen (Comet Lake), and 12th–15th Gen (Alder/Raptor/Raptor Refresh/Lunar/Arrow Lake).
x86-64-v4 — AMD 19h (Zen 4/Zen 4c), 1Ah (Zen 5/Zen 5c); Intel Skylake X, Cannon Lake, Ice/Cascade/Cooper Lake, Tiger/Sapphire/Emerald Rapids, Rocket Lake.

Relevant to Optimized Repositories and x86-64 Levels.
Writing the USB
balenaEtcher (Linux/macOS/Windows)
# Extract zip file:
bsdtar xvf <zip file name>
# cd to the new folder:
cd balenaEtcher-linux-x64/
# Execute balenaEtcher:
./balena-etcher
CLI (Linux & macOS)
Identify the drive first:
# Linux — the USB drive could be e.g. /dev/sda, by disk model and size
sudo fdisk -l
 
# macOS — USB drives are identified as /dev/diskN where N is 0,1,...
diskutil list
Then write it (replace <usbdrive> with the drive label):
sudo dd bs=4M if=full_iso_name.iso of=/dev/<usbdrive> status=progress oflag=sync
Rufus (Windows only)
Device -> Boot selection -> SELECT ISO -> START.
Ventoy (Linux & Windows)
# Replace version with the correct one, e.g. ventoy-1.1.07-linux.tar.gz
bsdtar xvf ventoy-version-linux.tar.gz
# cd to the new folder (version might change)
cd ventoy-1.1.07/
# It will ask for administrative privileges
./VentoyGUI.x86_64
Then place the ISO into the new usable partition of the drive.
Next: Installing CachyOS on a Desktop or Laptop.

cachyos/qemu-user-session.title: QEMU User Session
cachyos/qemu-user-session.content:
Part of CachyOS Wiki Notes. From the official CachyOS wiki (last updated 2025-11-24).
QEMU User Session
Why run a VM in a user session instead of a root session: networking and 3D acceleration via translation.
Networking
A root session forbids the VM from forwarding ports and uses NAT instead — the VM can see the world, but the world cannot see the VM, it sees your PC. Fine in general, but you cannot connect into the VM from outside the machine (e.g. over ssh), because there is nothing to connect to.
3D acceleration
A root session forbids VMM from using the render node /dev/dri/renderD128, and cripples qemu-cli — a regular user can barely make use of root qemu.
How to enable it

In the main VMM window, File -> Add Connection....
In the Hypervisor: dropdown, select QEMU/KVM user session.
Create VMs as described in QEMU and VMM Setup, in User mode rather than Root mode.

No packages, services, group changes, or config edits — the whole change is that one VMM connection setting.

cachyos/qemu-and-vmm-setup.title: QEMU and VMM Setup
cachyos/qemu-and-vmm-setup.content:
Part of CachyOS Wiki Notes. From the official CachyOS wiki (last updated 2026-03-08).
QEMU and VMM Setup
Installing Virtual Machine Manager (VMM) + QEMU on CachyOS.
Packages
qemu-full, virt-manager, swtpm.
swtpm is only needed for Windows 11 guests when you have no compatible TPM module to pass through — otherwise you can add a TPM later during configuration.
# Install the packages
sudo pacman -S qemu-full virt-manager swtpm
 
# Force libvirt to use iptables
echo 'firewall_backend = "iptables"' | sudo tee -a /etc/libvirt/network.conf
 
# Add the user to the libvirt group
sudo usermod -aG libvirt $USER
 
# LXC backend (optional, for Linux containers)
systemctl enable --now libvirtd.service
 
# QEMU backend (for VMs)
systemctl enable --now libvirtd.socket
 
# Bring Internet up in a VM whenever one starts
sudo virsh net-autostart default
 
# Let the whole VM subnet route out — consider tighter rules for your threat model
sudo ufw route allow from 192.168.122.0/24

Config file touched: /etc/libvirt/network.conf.
Both backends can be enabled at once; they do not conflict.
Before creating a VM, the wiki defers to QEMU User Session.

Creating a VM in VMM

Edit -> Preferences -> ✅ Enable XML editing.
New VM (star/play icon, or File -> New Virtual Machine), choose Connection:, locate the .iso via Browse... (add a dedicated ISO pool with + (Add Pool); the user-session pool path lives in ~/.config/libvirt/).
If the OS is not autodetected, untick autodetection and pick the closest match manually (CachyOS = Arch Linux).
Set RAM and CPU cores (changeable later), create virtual storage (makes a .qcow2) or give a path.
Tick Customize configuration before install -> Finish.
Linux guests: in Overview confirm chipset Q35 and firmware UEFI.
Windows 11: confirm a TPM is present, else Add Hardware -> TPM (Emulated or Passthrough), then Finish.
Click Begin Installation.
Guest uses OpenGL and/or ships libvulkan → see EGL Headless 3D Acceleration and Virtio-Venus 3D Acceleration respectively.

Windows 11 performance notes

Install Virtio-Win drivers (RedHat) inside the guest.
Intel iGPU: look into GVT-g and MDEV. Intel iGPU + dGPU: GVT-d.
dGPU passthrough (iGPU + dGPU, or 2+ dGPUs): VFIO.

cachyos/secure-boot-setup.title: Secure Boot Setup
cachyos/secure-boot-setup.content:
Part of CachyOS Wiki Notes. From the official CachyOS wiki (last updated 2026-08-25).
Secure Boot Setup
GRUB: enable secure boot support with CA keys

Warning from the wiki: loading unnecessary modules in your boot manager has the potential to present a security risk. Only run this if you actually need Secure Boot.

sudo grub-install --target=x86_64-efi --efi-directory=/boot/efi --bootloader-id=cachyos --modules="tpm" --disable-shim-lock
Enter firmware settings
systemctl reboot --firmware-setup
Set Secure Boot mode to “Setup Mode” (or “reset to setup mode” / restore factory keys).

Gigabyte: reject the “reset without saving” dialog after “reset to setup mode” — it disables setup mode. Instead use Save & Exit → boot override.
No Setup Mode — MSI: Secure Boot Mode = “custom”, select “maximum security” compatibility, then Key Management.
ASUS: Boot → Secure Boot → mode Custom → Key Management → “Delete all Secure Boot Variables”.

sbctl (the key manager)
sudo sbctl status
sudo sbctl create-keys
sudo sbctl enroll-keys --microsoft --firmware-builtin

Gotcha: on ASUS/Gigabyte, --firmware-builtin can create duplicate EFI key entries (builtin-db repeated) → Secure Boot Violation. Use only:

sudo sbctl enroll-keys --microsoft

If Vendor Keys shows microsoft builtin-db builtin-db ..., re-enter Setup Mode (delete all keys) and re-run sbctl enroll-keys --microsoft.

Re-check sudo sbctl status. If Setup Mode shows Enabled, temporarily disable Secure Boot in firmware, boot back, sign, reboot, and re-enable.
Limine
Only Limine’s EFI binary needs signing — its boot process bypasses EFI chainloading/signature checks, so do not sign images with sbctl-batch-sign (see CachyOS Settings Package).
From Limine 11.2.0 Secure Boot is strictly enforced: a BLAKE2B config checksum must be enrolled (otherwise panic SECURE BOOT IS ACTIVE BUT NO CONFIG CHECKSUM IS ENROLLED), all limine.conf paths need BLAKE2B hashes (boot():/vmlinuz-linux#<hash>), the config editor is disabled, and a hash mismatch panics.
Enable in /etc/default/limine:
ENABLE_ENROLL_LIMINE_CONFIG=yes

Hash the splash image and append the hash to its path in /boot/limine.conf:
sudo b2sum /boot/limine-splash.png
wallpaper: boot():/limine-splash.png#75205d08fa9c61599897857e861d6b2f6da25465183fc4cc9efecffb22ee630efb510f2ef1b17677db94c28d5c69ad2ceb4d3892f5bec9cfa65c97b5ba16f52f

Then:
sudo limine-enroll-config
sudo limine-update
Verify
sudo sbctl status
bootctl
bootctl should show Secure Boot: enabled (user).
fwupd with Secure Boot
Sign the UEFI executable:
sudo sbctl sign -s -o /usr/lib/fwupd/efi/fwupdx64.efi.signed /usr/lib/fwupd/efi/fwupdx64.efi
And add to /etc/fwupd/fwupd.conf:
[uefi_capsule]
DisableShimForSecureBoot=true

Related: CachyOS Boot Managers, Boot Manager Configuration.

cachyos/switching-between-nvidia-and-amd.title: Switching Between NVIDIA and AMD GPUs
cachyos/switching-between-nvidia-and-amd.content:
Part of CachyOS Wiki Notes. From the official CachyOS wiki (last updated 2026-09-15).
Switching Between NVIDIA and AMD GPUs
Prerequisites: the replacement GPU is properly installed and connected, and the system is fully up to date:
sudo pacman -Syu
NVIDIA → AMD, in order


Make a note of your username and password — you may need to log in via TTY.


Check which NVIDIA driver profile is installed:
sudo chwd --list-installed


Remove that profile with -r:
sudo chwd -r <profile-name>


Shut down and install the AMD GPU. If the system lands on a black screen, press CTRL+ALT+F3 to reach a TTY and log in (mind NUMLOCK).


After booting, let chwd detect the GPU and install the AMD packages:
sudo chwd -a


Update the initramfs and bootloader config. CachyOS ships a pacman hook that rebuilds the initramfs automatically when drivers are added/removed, so the right drivers load at boot:

GRUB — sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg
systemd-boot — sudo sdboot-manage gen
Limine — sudo limine-mkinitcpio

See Boot Manager Configuration.


Reboot:
sudo reboot


Verify the AMD drivers are active:
vulkaninfo | grep "deviceName"
or
glxinfo | grep "OpenGL renderer"
If your AMD GPU is listed, they are working.



Caveat: the wiki page is a tabbed guide (“From NVIDIA to AMD” / “From AMD to NVIDIA”). Only the NVIDIA→AMD tab body was recoverable — do not assume the reverse direction mirrors it. AMD drivers are in the kernel, so going AMD→NVIDIA is mainly cleaning up old config, but check the page for its own steps.

Related: Managing Hardware with chwd, Dual GPU Setup.

cachyos/switching-desktop-environments.title: Switching Desktop Environments
cachyos/switching-desktop-environments.content:
Part of CachyOS Wiki Notes. From the official CachyOS wiki (last updated 2026-07-25).
Switching Desktop Environments
Things to consider

Multiple DEs/WMs can conflict — especially settings managers, default applications, and appearance configs such as GTK/Qt themes and icons. The two worst offenders are GNOME and KDE Plasma (different toolkits — GTK vs Qt — plus many background services).
Package bloat matters for mainstream DEs (hundreds of packages).
Window managers mix with DEs more easily, e.g. KDE Plasma + Hyprland, picked at login.

How CachyOS settings packages work
Each CachyOS-offered DE/WM has its own -settings package, e.g. cachyos-i3wm-settings. These place config files in /etc/skel/ — the template used for new user accounts.

Important: for existing users these settings are NOT applied automatically, to avoid overwriting personal configs.

Two install choices:

Keep your current config files and manually adjust/copy from /etc/skel as needed (e.g. copy only i3wm-related files from /etc/skel/.config/i3 into your home directory).
Overwrite your configs with the ones from /etc/skel/ for the full CachyOS experience.

Procedure


Back up your current configs:
mkdir -p ~/config-backup
cp -r ~/.config ~/config-backup/
cp -r ~/.local ~/config-backup/


Uninstall the current -settings package, e.g. KDE:
sudo pacman -R cachyos-kde-settings
This does not remove your current DE/WM configurations — only the files stored in /etc/skel.


Install the new DE/WM plus its -settings package, e.g. i3wm:
sudo pacman -Syu i3-wm cachyos-i3wm-settings
Available DEs/WMs and packages: github.com/CachyOS/CachyOS-PKGBUILDS.


Copy the new config files from /etc/skel into your home directory. Example: cachyos-i3wm-settings carries config for Kvantum, dunst, GTK, i3, polybar, Qt5 and rofi.

File manager route: enable hidden files (Ctrl+H, or View → Show Hidden Files), go to /etc/skel, select all (Ctrl+A), copy (Ctrl+C), go to your home directory, paste (Ctrl+V), then choose “Merge”/“Apply to All” for folders and “Replace” for individual files you want to update — careful, this overwrites current configs.
Or do it in the terminal.



Log out; at the login screen pick the newly installed DE/WM from the session options before logging back in.


FAQ


Reverting to your previous config — restore from the backup:
cp -r ~/config-backup/.config/* ~/.config/
cp -r ~/config-backup/.local/* ~/.local/


New updates to a -settings package — new files go to /etc/skel/, your user config in /home/ stays untouched; apply updates by copying from /etc/skel/ again. Watch the relevant GitHub repo.


Can I install multiple -settings packages? Yes and no — multiple DEs/WMs can be installed, but only one -settings package at a time is recommended to avoid conflicts in /etc/skel/; otherwise pacman may complain about file conflicts.


What are “CachyOS Settings”? Convenience configuration packages for various DEs/WMs providing pre-configured settings, themes and tweaks. Installing one also pulls in dependencies the vanilla DE/WM doesn’t ship, such as themes, icons, wallpapers and extra apps — e.g. cachyos-i3wm-settings installs rofi, dunst, picom, lxappearance and more.


Maintained repos: KDE Plasma CachyOS/cachyos-kde-settings, GNOME CachyOS/cachyos-gnome-settings, Niri cachyos/cachyos-niri-noctalia, Hyprland CachyOS/cachyos-hypr-noctalia, MangoWM CachyOS/cachyos-mangowc-dms, i3 CachyOS/cachyos-i3wm-settings, Qtile CachyOS/cachyos-qtile-settings, Wayfire CachyOS/cachyos-wayfire-settings. All other offered DEs/WMs have no -settings package yet (vanilla versions).
Related: KDE Plasma on CachyOS, Niri Keybinds and FAQ, Hyprland Setup and Keybinds, i3 Keybinds and FAQ, Qtile Keybinds and FAQ.

cachyos/virtio-venus-3d-acceleration.title: Virtio-Venus 3D Acceleration
cachyos/virtio-venus-3d-acceleration.content:
Part of CachyOS Wiki Notes. From the official CachyOS wiki (last updated 2025-11-24).
Virtio-Venus (near-native 3D acceleration)

URL note: /virtualization/virtio_venus/ (underscore) 404s — the live page is the hyphenated slug /virtualization/virtio-venus/.

For guests that use libvulkan — Linux, BSDs, Android — you can get near-native performance by translating calls from the VM to Vulkan, then directly to the GPU and back, without passing the GPU through to the VM.
Limitation: Virtio-Venus is not exposed in VMM, so it requires qemu-cli. You need to know the VM’s name and where it lives.
Example invocation
qemu-system-x86_64                                                                             \
    -enable-kvm                                                                                \
    -M q35                                                                                     \
    -smp 6                                                                                     \
    -m 12G                                                                                     \
    -cpu host                                                                                  \
    -net nic,model=virtio                                                                      \
    -net user,hostfwd=tcp::2222-:22                                                            \
    -device virtio-sound-pci,audiodev=my_audiodev -audiodev pipewire,id=my_audiodev            \
    -device virtio-vga-gl,hostmem=4G,blob=true,venus=true                                      \
    -vga none                                                                                  \
    -display gtk,gl=on,show-cursor=on                                                          \
    -usb -device usb-tablet                                                                    \
    -object memory-backend-memfd,id=mem1,size=12G                                              \
    -machine memory-backend=mem1                                                               \
    -drive if=pflash,format=raw,readonly=on,file=/usr/share/edk2/x64/OVMF_CODE.secboot.4m.fd   \
    -drive if=pflash,format=raw,file=.config/libvirt/qemu/nvram/archlinux_VARS.fd              \
    -drive file=.local/share/libvirt/images/archlinux.qcow2
Flags explained


-smp 6 — 6 CPU cores.


-m 12G — 12 GB RAM.


-net user,hostfwd=tcp::2222-:22 — forwards guest port 22 to host port 2222:
ssh -p 2222 vmusername@vmipaddress


-device virtio-vga-gl,hostmem=4G,blob=true,venus=true — the Venus driver, not yet in virt-manager; once it is, everything here except user mode is superseded. hostmem=4G lets the VM use up to 4 GB of your VRAM.


-object memory-backend-memfd,id=mem1,size=12G — size must match the RAM you gave the VM.


-drive if=pflash,...OVMF_CODE.secboot.4m.fd — the firmware file path.


-drive if=pflash,format=raw,file=.config/libvirt/qemu/nvram/archlinux_VARS.fd — the VM’s nvram; without it (or if read-only) the VM won’t run.


-drive file=.local/share/libvirt/images/archlinux.qcow2 — the VM’s storage.


Audio uses pipewire instead of ich9 in the example; the page says that detail is irrelevant.

cachyos/why-cachyos.title: Why CachyOS
cachyos/why-cachyos.content:
Part of CachyOS Wiki Notes. From the official CachyOS wiki (last updated 2026-01-27).
Why CachyOS
A performance-centric Arch Linux distribution: rolling release with a custom toolchain.
Optimized packages and repositories

A large selection of packages recompiled for modern CPU architectures: x86-64-v3, x86-64-v4, and Zen4+ — see Optimized Repositories and x86-64 Levels.
Package browser: packages.cachyos.org/.

Custom kernel

The CachyOS base kernel patch set tunes kernel parameters to improve desktop responsiveness.
Cherry-picks patch sets that are not mainlined or not in the kernel stable revision; these get internal testing before release so stability is not impacted. See CachyOS Kernels.

CPU scheduler support

EEVDF (the default Linux scheduler): the CachyOS kernel carries custom EEVDF tunables to improve desktop responsiveness (throughput-oriented by default).
BORE (Burst-Oriented Response Enhancer, github.com/firelzrd/bore-scheduler): enhances EEVDF for a more fluid experience under heavy workloads — for maximum interactivity. Ships in the linux-cachyos-bore variant. See sched-ext Schedulers.

User-friendly tools

Custom hardware detection automatically identifies and installs the necessary drivers and packages, removing manual driver hunting after install.
The installer lets you choose desktop environment, packages, filesystem, boot manager, kernel and more. Custom-package list source: github.com/CachyOS/cachyos-calamares/blob/cachyos-limine-qt6/src/modules/netinstall/netinstall.yaml.

CachyOS-maintained applications

CachyOS Hello (github.com/CachyOS/CachyOS-Welcome) — welcome app for tweaks, fixes, and package installs.
CachyOS Package Installer (github.com/CachyOS/packageinstaller) — GUI for installing applications.
CachyOS Kernel Manager (github.com/CachyOS/kernel-manager) — install repo kernels, configure your own, manage the sched-ext framework.
cachyos-rate-mirrors (github.com/CachyOS/rate-mirrors) — ranks Arch and CachyOS mirrors for optimal pacman download speed.
systemd-boot-manager (github.com/CachyOS/systemd-boot-manager) — auto-generates new systemd-boot entries; configured via /etc/sdboot-manage.conf.

Community
Discord discord.gg/cachyos-862292009423470592 and forum discuss.cachyos.org.

cachyos/cachy-chroot-recovery-helper.title: cachy-chroot Recovery Helper
cachyos/cachy-chroot-recovery-helper.content:
Part of CachyOS Wiki Notes. From the official CachyOS wiki (last updated 2026-07-25).
cachy-chroot Recovery Helper
cachy-chroot (github.com/CachyOS/cachy-chroot) chroots into an existing CachyOS or Arch-based install.

Lists every partition found on the machine, supports listing BTRFS subvolumes, and supports encrypted systems via LUKS.
Maps each fstab entry to its crypttab entry and gracefully closes all LUKS volumes on exit.
Supports essentially any filesystem the Linux kernel supports — except ZFS.

Usage
Navigate with arrow keys, select with ENTER. ❯ marks the current selection; ? means it’s prompting for input.


Boot a CachyOS live ISO.


Open a terminal and become root: sudo su.


Make sure you have the latest version:
pacman -Sy cachy-chroot


Run it:
cachy-chroot
It scans and lists all available partitions.


Select the partition holding the root filesystem.


It tries to auto-mount every partition and subvolume listed in the root device’s /etc/fstab. Failed mounts are reported and can be mounted manually; answer no to skip.


You are in the chroot; the prompt looks like:
[root@CachyOS /]#

Example maintenance commands:
pacman -Syu
mkinitcpio -P


Exit with exit or CTRL+D.


On exit it cleans up mounted partitions and closes LUKS containers, returning you to the live shell.


Troubleshooting

No partitions found — make sure the disk is connected and recognized by the live system; check lsblk or fdisk -l.
Automount fails for some partitions — mount them manually from inside the chroot; cachy-chroot ignores failures and continues.

FAQ

Mounting extra partitions — useful for a broken/missing fstab (mount /boot or /home manually to repair or recover data), or after partition UUIDs changed (mount and fix fstab when the system won’t boot).
Arch Wiki chroot reference: wiki.archlinux.org/title/Chroot.

Related: CachyOS FAQ and Troubleshooting (bootloader recovery walks through this).

cachyos/sched-ext-schedulers.title: sched-ext Schedulers
cachyos/sched-ext-schedulers.content:
Part of CachyOS Wiki Notes. From the official CachyOS wiki (last updated 2026-09-07).
sched-ext Schedulers
sched-ext (Extensible Scheduler Class) is a Linux kernel feature for implementing thread schedulers in BPF and loading them dynamically — you swap schedulers from userspace without building a new kernel.
Running any sched-ext scheduler temporarily detaches the default kernel scheduler (EEVDF or BORE); stopping it hands control back.
Packages
Schedulers come from scx-scheds / scx-scheds-git:
# Stable branch + scx_loader and scxctl tools
sudo pacman -S scx-scheds scx-tools
 
# Bleeding edge + tools
sudo pacman -S scx-scheds-git scx-tools-git
scx-scheds-git may not include every experimental scheduler (some live in unmerged feature branches). Both scxctl and scx_loader need admin rights (sudo, or a polkit agent that prompts).
Run one from a terminal
sudo scx_rusty
CTRL + C stops it and the default scheduler takes over again.
scxctl (runtime control, needs a working polkit agent)
scxctl start --sched flash --mode gaming
scxctl stop
scxctl restore
scxctl switch --sched bpfland --mode gaming
scxctl start --sched cosmos --args="-c,75,-m,0-15"
scxctl switch --sched flash --args="-s,20000"
Arguments are comma-separated, e.g. --args="-c,75,-m,0-15" is argument,value pairs. Subcommands: get, list, start, switch, stop, restart, restore. scxctl restore returns to the default scheduler from the config file.
scx_loader D-Bus interface
dbus-send --system --print-reply --dest=org.scx.Loader /org/scx/Loader org.scx.Loader.StartScheduler string:scx_rusty uint32:0

Mode numbers: 0 = default scheduler flags, 1 = Gaming, 2 = Power Saving, 3 = Low Latency, 4 = Server. Other methods: StartSchedulerWithArgs, StopScheduler, RestoreDefault, SwitchScheduler, SwitchSchedulerWithArgs, plus property reads CurrentScheduler / SupportedSchedulers.
Setting a default scheduler at boot
sudo mkdir -p /etc/scx_loader
sudo cp /usr/share/scx_loader/config.toml /etc/scx_loader/config.toml
sudo nano /etc/scx_loader/config.toml
Set default_sched = "scx_pandemonium", default_mode = "Auto", then:
sudo systemctl enable --now scx_loader.service
Config lookup order: /etc/scx_loader/config.toml (preferred) → /etc/scx_loader.toml → /usr/share/scx_loader/config.toml → /usr/share/scx_loader.toml. Per-scheduler arguments go under a [scheds.scx_name] section.

Gotcha: do not run scx_loader.service alongside scx.service — the loader starts but does nothing.

systemctl disable --now scx.service && systemctl enable --now scx_loader.service
systemctl restart scx_loader.service
The old scx.service (SCX_SCHEDULER=, SCX_FLAGS=) maps to default_sched = "scx_lavd" / default_mode = "Auto" plus [scheds.scx_lavd] with auto_mode = ["--performance"]. The Kernel Manager GUI handles the transition unless you had custom flags in /etc/default/scx — see CachyOS Kernel Manager.
Debugging
systemctl status scx_loader.service
journalctl -u scx_loader.service
journalctl -u scx_loader.service -b 0
ananicy-cpp usually coexists fine; disable it as a troubleshooting step for stalls: systemctl disable --now ananicy-cpp.
Power-profile switching (patched power-profiles-daemon): Power Saver → Power Save, Balanced → Auto, Performance → Gaming. The game-performance wrapper switches to Gaming on game launch and reverts on close.
Benchmarking
sudo pacman -S cachyos-benchmarker
cachyos-benchmarker ~/cachyos-benchmarker/
 
sudo pacman -S schbench
schbench -m 2 -t 8 -r 60
Crash log:
journalctl --unit scx_loader.service --boot 0 > crash.log
Schedulers documented on the page
scx_beerland, scx_bpfland, scx_cake, scx_cosmos, scx_flash, scx_flow, scx_forge, scx_lavd, scx_pandemonium, scx_p2dq, scx_tickless, scx_rustland, scx_rusty.
Each scheduler lists per-mode flags where it has them; use scx_<schedulername> --help for the real list. No modes are listed for scx_beerland (“none for the moment”), scx_cake, scx_forge, scx_rustland or scx_rusty. Example flags: bpfland Low Latency -m performance -w, Power Save -s 20000 -m powersave -I 100 -t 100; cosmos Gaming -s 700 -S; LAVD --performance / --powersave (plus scx_lavd --autopower); p2dq Gaming --task-slice true -f --sched-mode performance. scx_flow has no Gaming/Power Save/Low Latency modes.
Related: CachyOS Kernels (BORE/EEVDF/BMQ variants), CachyOS Kernel Manager.

camera-pose-tracker-findings.title: Camera pose tracker findings
camera-pose-tracker-findings.content:
Camera pose tracker findings
Building a webcam body tracker (skeleton only, camera feed never displayed) for a friend on Windows. Project lives at /OpenCode-Sandbox/camera-pose.
YOLO pose vs MediaPipe

YOLO pose gives 17 COCO keypoints only: nose, eyes, ears, shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles. No hands/fingers, no face detail, and partial arms are unreliable.
For hands, face, and partial arms use MediaPipe tasks API (installed 1.1.1):

vision.PoseLandmarker → 33 points (includes refined arms)
vision.HandLandmarker → 21 points per hand, num_hands=2
vision.FaceLandmarker → 468-point face mesh + irises


MediaPipe 1.x has no mp.solutions — that API is gone. Use mediapipe.tasks + .task model assets.
.task models auto-download from storage.googleapis.com/mediapipe-models/....
Drawing: vision.drawing_utils.draw_landmarks + PoseLandmarksConnections.POSE_LANDMARKS, HandLandmarksConnections.HAND_CONNECTIONS, FaceLandmarksConnections.FACE_LANDMARKS_* (all 0-based, unlike ultralytics’ 1-based skeleton list).

Windows gotchas (friend’s machine)

MediaPipe wheels are py3-none-win_amd64 — they work on Python 3.14. The 3.12 advice was wrong; no need to downgrade.
opencv-python vs opencv-contrib-python conflict: MediaPipe depends on opencv-contrib-python, which also provides cv2. Installing both breaks the import chain and shows as “No module named mediapipe”. Fix: pip uninstall -y opencv-python opencv-contrib-python then pip install mediapipe (it pulls its own opencv).
Virtual camera: pyvirtualcam on Windows needs the OBS Virtual Camera driver. Run OBS Studio once to register it; then select “OBS Virtual Camera” in Discord/Zoom.
Em-dash trap: Windows errors “No such file or directory” when a path contains an em-dash (camera—pose) instead of a hyphen (camera-pose). Use hyphen-free folder names.
One-liner pattern that works: download zip → Expand-Archive to %USERPROFILE%\Downloads → pip install mediapipe pyvirtualcam → run py <full path>\script.py --virtual.

Linux virtual camera

v4l2loopback: pkexec modprobe v4l2loopback devices=1 video_nr=2 card_label="BodyTrack" exclusive_caps=1 creates /dev/video2.
Feed it by piping raw BGR frames to ffmpeg -f rawvideo -pix_fmt bgr24 -s WxH -r 30 -i - -f v4l2 /dev/video2.
pkexec rmmod v4l2loopback removes it. A consumer (Discord) left pointing at a dead virtual camera can spin and lag the machine — switch its camera to None first.

Performance

MediaPipe runs on CPU, not the GPU. Heavy pose + face mesh + hands is slow.
Fast preset: pose_landmarker_lite only, ~256px input, single model.
Complex preset: pose_landmarker_heavy + both hands + full face mesh, 640px.

Privacy invariant
The overlay/virtual camera must only ever contain landmarks on black. Never pass the captured frame to the drawing surface; capture is for inference only. Mirror the canvas at the end (cv2.flip(canvas, 1)).

graph-guide.title: Graph Guide
graph-guide.content:
Graph Guide
How to build the graph by hand — one note, one [[link]], at a time.


                  
                  The one-sentence version 
                  
                

The graph is nothing but your links. No links → lonely dots. Links → edges. Everything below is a way of adding more edges.


1. A note is just a file
Every note is a plain .md file in this folder. That’s it. Rename the file, the note changes. Delete it, the note’s gone.

New note: Ctrl+N
Or: click any [[link]] to a note that doesn’t exist yet — Obsidian creates it for you (this is the fastest way to grow).

2. The link syntax — this is the whole trick

































You typeYou get[[Note Name]]A link to that note (and an edge in the graph)[[Note Name|shown text]]Same link, displays “shown text”[[Note Name#Heading]]Jumps to a heading inside that note[[Note Name^block-id]]Jumps to a specific block![[Note Name]]Embeds the whole note inline (transclusion)[[Brand New Note]]Doesn’t exist? Click it → creates the note
3. Making an edge
Two ways links happen:

You write it. Type [[ anywhere in a note and Obsidian pops an autocomplete of every note you can link to.
Backlinks (automatic). You only ever write one direction. If A links to B, Obsidian automatically shows A in B’s Backlinks panel (right sidebar). So:

Outgoing links = what this note points to.
Backlinks = what points to this note.
You never have to write the reverse link yourself.



4. The build loop (do this on repeat)
open a note  →  ask "what does this connect to?"  →  type [[target]]
     ↑                                                        │
     └──────────  click it, create it if missing  ←───────────┘

That’s the entire craft. Open Inbox. Think “what’s this related to?” — type [[. Pick or create. Move to the new note. Repeat. Ten minutes of this and your graph looks alive.
5. The graph view

Ctrl+G → whole-vault graph.
Local graph → Ctrl+P → “Open local graph”. Shows only this note’s neighborhood. This one is actually useful; the big one is eye candy.
Color it: top-right of graph → Groups → + → type a query, pick a color. Examples:

tag:#project
tag:#guide
path:Daily


Filters: the graph panel can also filter by search text, hide orphans, show tags.

6. Tags & frontmatter — structure the graph
Tags let you color, filter, and query. Put them in the frontmatter at the very top:
---
tags:
  - project
  - guide
created: 2026-10-15
---
Or inline, anywhere in the text: #project.
Tags are how the color Groups know what to paint. Link = edge; tag = category. Together they turn a hairball into a map.
7. Hygiene — the two things to watch

Dangling links (show up in a different color, “unresolved”): you linked to a note that doesn’t exist. Either click to create it, or delete the link. Not an error — a to-do.
Orphans: notes with no links in or out. They float alone. Fix by linking them into something. (Frontmatter/tags don’t count as links.)

8. Naming rules (save yourself pain)

Filenames must be unique for short [[links]] to work.
Spaces are fine — [[Graph Guide]] works.
Renaming a note: Obsidian can auto-update every link pointing to it (enable Options → Files & Links → Automatically update internal links).

9. Practice — go do it now

Make a note (Ctrl+N), name it anything. Add the line See also: [[Graph Guide]] and save. Watch the edge appear in the graph.
Open two notes you care about and link them together.
Hit Ctrl+G, then open the local graph of the note with the most links.



                  
                  The trap 
                  
                

The graph is the most fun part of Obsidian and the least valuable. Pretty dots aren’t knowledge — links are. A thousand linked notes is a brain; a thousand colored dots is a screensaver. Play for five minutes, then go write.

kimaki/kimaki-internals.title: Kimaki Internals
kimaki/kimaki-internals.content:
Kimaki Internals
Part of Kimaki. Distilled from the repo’s AGENTS.md — the maintainer’s rules for working on Kimaki (bot + CLI, built on OpenCode V2).
Repo shape
The important package is kimaki/: the Discord bot and the kimaki CLI (npm kimaki), built on OpenCode V2 only. The legacy V1 codebase lives in cli/ on the v1 branch (git show v1:cli/<path>) and is never re-added here. kimaki/CHANGELOG.md keeps the V1 history.
Other packages: gateway-proxy/ (Rust, multi-tenant Discord Gateway + REST proxy, hosted on Fly.io), website/ (kimaki.dev — OAuth callback + onboarding status), db/ (shared Postgres/Prisma schema for website + gateway; the bot itself doesn’t use it).
kimaki/ (bot + CLI, local SQLite) ──REST+WS (clientId:secret)──▶ gateway-proxy/ (Rust, fly.io) ──▶ Discord
   │    │                                                             ▲ polls every 1s
   │    └─ polls /api/onboarding/status ──▶ website/ (CF Worker) ──▶ shared Postgres (db/)
   └── one /api/event stream + HTTP client ──▶ user's shared OpenCode V2 service (not bot-owned)

Bot data flow:
Discord msg ─▶ ingress.ts ─▶ prompt.ts / sessions.ts ─▶ OpenCode (session.prompt, create, interrupt)
OpenCode ev ─▶ opencode-server.ts ─▶ event-loop.ts ─▶ thread-reducer.ts (pure) ─▶ effects.ts ─▶ Discord

Key modules: main.ts (wiring: lock port → SQLite migration → OpenCode + Discord login in parallel) · bot.ts/store.ts (context + the one zustand store) · ingress.ts (messages, attachments, voice) · slash-commands.ts + commands/* · opencode-server.ts (service discovery, event subscription, plugin shim) · event-loop.ts + thread-reducer.ts (pure fold → view + effects) · effects.ts (the only Discord writer for session output) · lock-server.ts/lock-routes.ts (single-instance lock + local HTTP API for CLI subcommands) · cli.ts + cli/* (goke CLI) · plugin/ (runs inside the OpenCode process) · autostart.ts.
Build rule: after every change run pnpm build (tsc) inside kimaki — the plugin autostarts the bot from dist/cli.js, so stale dist runs old code. Try never to use as any.
OpenCode SDK rules
Kimaki runs on native OpenCode V2. Import the client from @opencode/client, plugin types from @opencode/plugin. Never import @opencode-ai/sdk (v1). Calls use flat inputs and return results or reject — no V1 .data/.error wrapper; paginated results carry data + cursor.

session.create({ location: { directory }, permissions })
session.prompt({ sessionID, text, files, delivery }) returns the inbox item, not the reply
session.interrupt({ sessionID }) (was session.abort)
message.list({ sessionID, order, cursor, limit }), session.list(...) — paginated

In the bot, call OpenCode through oc(bot, 'operation.name', (client) => ...), turning rejections into OpenCodeError values.
Kimaki uses the user’s shared OpenCode service, not a bot-owned server. opencode-server.ts discovers it or starts it via Service.ensure() (binary search: OPENCODE_PATH, then opencode, ~/.opencode/bin/opencode, then the rare opencode2; minimum version enforced). OpenCode is not bundled and versions are never pinned — that would replace the running server and kill the user’s TUI sessions. For OpenCode questions, read the source from anomalyco/opencode (not opencode-ai/opencode, an unrelated repo).
Prompt cache
OpenCode V2 keeps the system prompt stable until compaction starts a new instruction epoch, so the provider cache keeps hitting. Put session-level text in instruction entries (session.instructions.entry.put), never in the plugin context hook: event.system.push(...) runs on every request and sits before all messages, so any change invalidates the whole cached prefix. Only push text there that stays constant during a session. Kimaki prints -# ⬦ prompt cache miss: ... when the cached prefix of a root step shrinks.
Gateway REST safety
When running with client_id:secret through gateway-proxy, Discord REST calls must be guild-scoped or explicitly allowlisted. Avoid global application routes like /applications/{app_id}/commands; use /applications/{app_id}/guilds/{guild_id}/commands. Invariants:

Never let client-authenticated requests hit unscoped bot-token routes.
Only tokenized interaction/webhook routes are allowed without auth (/interactions/{id}/{token}/…, /webhooks/{id}/{token}/…).
Never treat /webhooks/{id} as allowlisted.
For AllowedWithoutAuth routes, don’t inject bot Authorization upstream.
Fail closed (403/401) when route scope can’t be proven guild-scoped or token-scoped.

Running & restarting

Only restart the bot if the user explicitly asks. kimaki restart — the root process supervises the bot as a child and respawns it with on-disk code; sessions keep running in OpenCode.
Single-instance lock on KIMAKI_LOCK_PORT (default 29988). A second bot on the same port stops the running one (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 20s) and takes the port. To run alongside the main bot: KIMAKI_LOCK_PORT=31001 kimaki --data-dir ~/.kimaki-test. CLI subcommands need the same port as their target bot.
kimaki profile cpu / kimaki profile heap write profiles to <dataDir>/profiles/.

SQLite
State persists between runs, and the DB must never have breaking changes — new Kimaki must keep working with older SQLite databases; if not, ask the user before adding a startup migration.

File <dataDir>/kimaki.db (libSQL + Drizzle, db.ts); only the bot start migrates (openDb({ migrate: true })), subcommands never do.
Schema kimaki/src/schema.ts; pnpm generate writes src/schema-sql.ts (idempotent CREATE … IF NOT EXISTS) — never edit by hand.
Migrations live in kimaki/src/migrations.ts. First start imports the V1 discord-sessions.db read-only. PRAGMA user_version marks a Kimaki-made DB.
New columns on existing tables: IF NOT EXISTS skips the whole CREATE, so also add an ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN (ignoring “duplicate column”) — and run the ALTER before schema statements if a generated index uses the new column, else existing DBs crash with no such column. Add a db.test.ts case over an old-shaped DB (fixtures/v1-schema.sql).
Inline straightforward Drizzle queries at the call site; no repository layer.

Plugin (runs inside OpenCode)
kimaki/src/plugin/ runs in the OpenCode server process, not the bot. On start the bot writes a shim per plugin into <opencode config dir>/plugins/<name>/index.js re-exporting dist/plugin/. Writing the shim only when content changes matters: any change in that folder reloads every location and cancels pending forms. Each plugin is a directory loaded through its index module; OpenCode keeps one plugin per ID (Duplicate plugin ID otherwise).

plugin/index.ts (kimaki): git-branch reminder, <discord-user> turn context, extra tool inputs, shell env, file-edit log.
plugin/anthropic/index.ts (kimaki-anthropic): Claude Pro/Max OAuth for every session, TUI included.

The kimaki plugin must only act on Kimaki sessions — OpenCode loads it for every session. Each hook first checks the session’s metadata.kimaki marker (or the parent chain for subagents) and returns unchanged when missing. Exceptions: the built-in skills and the stable <dataDir>/bin shell shim. The plugin gets bot state from the marker, not env vars (dataDir, lockPort), and never gets the bot token. Plugin files must not import logger.ts/db.ts or anything pulling in discord.js/SQLite, and must never write to stdout/stderr — fail silently.
Logging
Always createLogger('PREFIX') from logger.ts, never console. Logs go to stderr, never stdout — stdout is only for command results (--json, tables, markdown), onboarding prompts/install URLs, and programmatic data: {…} events. Anything else breaks piped commands and leaks into the TUI. Logs also go to <dataDir>/kimaki.log (default ~/.kimaki/kimaki.log), reset on every bot start.
Discord constraints (hard-won)

Rate limits: global 50 req/s per bot; ~5 sends/5s and ~5 edits/5s per channel; thread rename 2 per 10 min; invalid requests 10k/10min per IP (then a temporary Cloudflare ban); interaction token valid 15 min. effects.ts keeps one FIFO worker per thread; merges consecutive bot lines when Discord is slower than the stream. Throttle live edits to ≤1/s (throttle, not debounce), serialize edits, new message past 2000 chars.
No TypeScript casts on Discord interaction objects (as GuildMember) — values arrive as hydrated classes or raw API payloads. Narrow at runtime or fetch the member (canUseKimaki()). Fail closed on missing context.
custom_id max 100 chars — store short IDs only, resolve the rest at interaction time (resolveTarget(bot, channelId) from interaction-context.ts). Never read the session location or channel row by hand in commands.
Message nonce max 25 chars — never send a raw UUID (NONCE_TYPE_TOO_LONG).
Components V2: max 40 components total (nested children count); no content/embeds; Section only 1–3 text children + one accessory; Action Row ≤5 buttons or one select; Container holds Action Row / Text Display / Section / Media Gallery / Separator / File. Don’t use Section for wide table rows (BASE_TYPE_BAD_LENGTH).
No emojis in bot messages; no blank lines between paragraphs in system messages.
Typing indicator: one pulse ≈10s; reducer emits typing on/off, effects.ts runs one 7s interval per thread. User messages never start typing — only OpenCode events do.

Message formatting lives in format-parts.ts: assistant text is plain Discord markdown, never quoted; tool lines are subtext (-# ┣ shell _ls_, edits use ◼︎); status lines use ⬦; errors start ✗ ; a successful turn gets a footer (-# *folder ⋅ branch ⋅ duration ⋅ % ⋅ model*) — never after interrupt/failure or while a subagent runs.
Testing

pnpm run test --run -u in kimaki after changes to message handling/queueing/reducer; inspect snapshot updates in git diff. One file: pnpm run test --run src/example.test.ts. (Always include run — pnpm test --run makes pnpm eat the flag.)
Each e2e file starts its own OpenCode server (~400 MB). vitest.config.ts caps parallel files at ⅓ of CPUs (KIMAKI_TEST_WORKERS). Run single files while iterating, the full suite once at the end.
Always assert on Discord messages, not internal state or logs. Prefer reusable actor/wait methods on DigitalDiscord (playwright-like). Add expect(await discord.thread(id).text()).toMatchInlineSnapshot() first in any test that creates/modifies messages, with deterministic content.
e2e uses opencode-deterministic-provider (model deterministic-v2) and canned turns; waitFor clamps timeouts to 8–10s. Snapshot only after waitForFooter (a -# *using …* banner is not a footer). Scope matchers with an explicit marker in the latest user text.

Product analytics (Strada)
Anonymous install-level events (bot_started, project_registered, session_created, turn_started, turn_completed, tokens_used) — no Discord IDs, paths, prompts, or secrets. Metrics are active installs, not people. Disable with kimaki --no-analytics or KIMAKI_STRADA_ENABLED=0 (off under vitest). Query with the strada CLI.
Debugging a session
Read the recorded events before guessing:
kimaki session events <sessionId|threadId> > ./tmp/events.jsonl
jq -r .event.type ./tmp/events.jsonl | sort | uniq -c
kimaki session read <id>          # messages as markdown
Thread events live in <dataDir>/session-events/<threadId>.jsonl and can be replayed with test/replay.ts.
Conventions & gotchas

errore submodule = errors-as-values; always on main, never detached. Read the errore skill before editing code; shared tagged errors in errors.ts.
CLI parsing uses goke, not cac — it infers option types from .option(), so never add manual type annotations to .action() callbacks.
Submodules (errore, gateway-proxy, traforo, opencode-injection-guard): push the submodule branch first, then bump the gitlink. Prove the remote has the SHA (gh api repos/remorses/<repo>/commits/<sha> --jq .sha) before changing a gitlink. Never force-push a submodule in a way that drops commits Kimaki still points at.
Never suggest installing from git (npm i -g remorses/kimaki#main) — it needs a build step. Point at the next npm release.
CLI startup must stay light (~0.06s, ~70 MB): kimaki/src/cli/*.ts must not top-level import SQLite modules or discord.js — await import() inside the actions that need them. Use discord-api-types/v10 for enums.

Not ported from V1 yet
Documentation must not claim these exist: self-upgrade (kimaki upgrade, /upgrade-and-restart) · sync-skills · the image-optimizer plugin · the kitty-graphics plugin (images printed by shell tools sent to Discord).

kimaki/index.title: Kimaki
kimaki/index.content:
Kimaki
A collaborative agent orchestrator that lives inside Discord, by Remorses (Tommy D. Rossi). It drives every feature of OpenCode (see Kimaki Internals) from Discord: each Discord channel is a project, each thread is a coding session. Send a message, an agent edits code on your machine.
Not a chat toy — the author runs all his development through it. Docs: kimaki.dev. Source: github.com/remorses/kimaki. Try it: Kimaki Discord.
Quick start
npx -y kimaki@latest
Setup is ~1 minute: install the bot to your server with one click, and Kimaki opens an onboarding thread where the agent asks which projects you want (one channel per project).
Requires OpenCode 2. If none is installed, Kimaki installs it (curl -fsSL opencode.ai/v2/install | bash). Had OpenCode 1? Install v2 first with the same command.
The model (why it’s split this way)
Other Discord/iMessage agent tools cram everything into one channel; sessions pile up. Kimaki maps work onto Discord’s native structure instead:

Channels are projects — linked to a directory on your machine.
Threads are sessions — every message starts a thread mapping to one OpenCode session.

Switch projects by switching channels, tasks by switching threads. Search, resume, and fork later.
Discord server            Your machine
#web-app  ─────────────▶  /code/web-app  ──▶ OpenCode session (thread)
#api      ─────────────▶  /code/api      ──▶ OpenCode session (thread)
   ▲ thread = session            │ agent reads/edits/runs in the project dir
   └── agent replies ◀───────────┘

Models & subscriptions
All models OpenCode supports (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, …). Crucially: use your existing Claude Pro/Max and ChatGPT/Codex subscriptions instead of per-token billing — run /login, pick a provider, choose OAuth. Logins are stored by OpenCode, so they work in Discord and the TUI. Kimaki adds Claude Pro/Max login to OpenCode via a small plugin.
Core features

Routines — run the bot on a schedule (cron or a future time). e.g. every morning read your inbox with Zele and post an email-digest thread.
The queue — queue a message for when the current run finishes. End any message with . queue (editable later) or use /queue.
btw — fork the current context into a new thread to ask a side question in parallel while the agent keeps working. . btw or /btw.
Worktrees — /new-worktree starts a session in an isolated git worktree; /merge-worktree merges back (rebase or squash).
Diff viewer — /diff generates a shareable review URL you can open from your phone.
Voice messages — record a voice note; transcribed using your project’s file tree for accuracy.
Voice calls — join the Kimaki voice channel and talk; GPT-Live answers on your ChatGPT subscription and a fast backend model starts/reads threads. Default voice cove; kimaki --voice juniper changes it (persisted in SQLite), --voice default resets.
Images / files — attach to a message; the agent can also upload files back into the thread.
OpenCode commands & skills — become Discord slash commands.
Shell commands — prefix a message with ! to run a shell command in the session folder.
Tunnels — expose a local dev server to a public URL (phone access).
Quick agent switching — swap model or system prompt with /<name>-agent.
Same sessions in the TUI — Kimaki uses your OpenCode 2 background service, so every session also opens in the OpenCode TUI. /session-id prints the command.

Message handling
A message sent during an active run interrupts it: Kimaki cancels pending questions and permission prompts, stops the run, and steers your new input in immediately. To wait instead, end with . queue or use /queue.
Commands





















































CommandDescription/resume <session>Resume a previous session (autocomplete)/abortStop the current running session/modelChange the AI model for this channel/session/agentChange the agent for this channel/session/loginAuthenticate a provider (OAuth subscription or API key)/queue <message>Queue a message for after the current response/btw <prompt>Fork context into a new thread for a side question/new-worktree <name>Start a session in an isolated git worktree/merge-worktreeMerge this worktree into a local branch/diffGenerate a shareable diff URL/session-idShow the session ID + the command to open it in the TUI
Full list: kimaki.dev/docs/reference/commands.
Setup modes

Gateway mode (default, recommended) — uses Kimaki’s pre-built Discord bot; no Developer Portal setup. One install link, authorize, done.
Self-hosted — make your own bot at discord.com/developers/applications (~5–10 min) for full control of the bot identity.

Both behave the same after setup. Keep the CLI running — it’s the bridge between Discord and your machine. Agents installing on a laptop/VPS should follow Set up Kimaki from an agent rather than cloning the repo.
Access control
A user needs one of: Server Owner · Manage Server · Administrator · a role literally named Kimaki (case-insensitive). Messages from anyone else are ignored. The Kimaki role is the recommended team approach.

Block a user with a role named no-kimaki — yes, even blocks server owners.
Other bots are ignored. For script/CI sessions use kimaki send.

Best practices

Run a dedicated Discord server for your agents.
Use the Kimaki role for team access.
Send long prompts as file attachments (“Send message as file”).

Troubleshooting

Sessions stop responding / won’t start → restart the OpenCode service: opencode service restart (Kimaki reconnects itself).
Bot itself broken (messages not picked up, no threads) → kimaki restart.
Update → npm i -g kimaki@latest, then kimaki restart.
Logs → kimaki logs (path printed; --follow tails).

Full guide: kimaki.dev/docs/guides/troubleshooting.

kimaki/other-remorses-projects.content:
Other Remorses Projects
Remorses = Tommy D. Rossi, Italy, @__morse on X — ~674 public repos, 1.2k followers, 5k+ stars. Same author as Kimaki. Themes: agent tooling, terminal UIs, and doing docs/dev-tooling the open way.
The big ones
Playwriter
Chrome extension + CLI (+ MCP) that lets agents drive your own running Chrome — your logins, cookies and extensions already there. Other browser MCPs spawn a fresh Chrome (no logins, no extensions, instantly bot-flagged, double the RAM); Playwriter connects to the browser you already have via an extension and a localhost WebSocket relay (:19988). One execute tool with the full Playwright API and persistent state across calls, Vimium-style accessibility labels, raw CDP, native video, tab groups, remote control (share your authenticated browser with a remote agent over a Cloudflare tunnel). ~4k★.
npm i -g playwriter
playwriter browser start
playwriter session new
playwriter -s 1 -e 'state.page = await context.newPage(); await state.page.goto("example.com")'

github.com/remorses/playwriter · playwriter.dev
Note: Chrome ignores --remote-debugging-port on your default profile since Chrome 136, so the extension route is the only one that keeps your real profile.
Telemetry goes to Strada (anonymous); opt out with PLAYWRITER_TELEMETRY=0 or DO_NOT_TRACK=1.

Holocron
Drop-in, open-source replacement for Mintlify as a Vite plugin. Same docs.json config shape, same MDX components, same frontmatter — migrate in ~2 minutes. Local vite build, deploy to Node/Cloudflare/holocron.so hosting; free vs Mintlify’s $150/mo. Ships AI-readable exports out of the box: .md route per page, /llms.txt, /docs.zip, and skill discovery at /.well-known/agent-skills/index.json. ~800★.
npx -y "@holocron.so/cli" create

github.com/remorses/holocron · holocron.so
Built on Spiceflow (React Server Components) + Tailwind; search via Orama; OpenAPI reference pages.

Termcast
Arc/Raycast-style TUI framework: build terminal apps with React using the Raycast extension API. Ports Raycast extensions (@raycast/api aliases to termcast at build time), hot module reloading via React Refresh, compiles to standalone executables, can even bundle a desktop app with an embedded terminal. Requires Bun (auto-respawns under bun if you run the TUI from a Node CLI). Terminal-only extras: braille charts, bar/stacked graphs, candlestick, calendar heatmap, tables. ~340★.
pnpm install -g termcast
termcast new my-extension
termcast dev

github.com/remorses/termcast · termcast.app
Profile TUIs with termcast dev + Bun --cpu-prof, analyze with profano (also his).

Critique
Terminal + web diff viewer. critique in the repo opens the working-tree diff in a TUI (split view, word-level diffs, Tree-sitter highlighting, watch mode, file switcher, click-to-open in $REACT_EDITOR); --web "title" uploads it to critique.work and prints a shareable URL with a .patch endpoint. Also: GitHub PR URLs without a checkout, --pdf for e-readers, --calldiff (call-stack diffs), critique hunks (stable hunk IDs for agents — a scriptable git add -p), password-protected links, critique pick from another branch. Bun-only. ~1.3k★.
bunx critique                      # working tree, TUI
critique --web "Fix auth retry"    # shareable URL
critique github.com/owner/repo/pull/19 --web "PR #19"

github.com/remorses/critique · critique.work
Uploads expire after 7 days without a license key; identical diffs reuse a content-hash URL.

gpuix
React and Solid for GPUI — Zed’s GPU UI framework. Write JSX/useState in TypeScript; GPUIX paints it with Metal / DirectX / Vulkan / WebGPU. No Electron, no web view. A napi-rs native bridge (Rust RetainedTree) plus a browser wasm build; the framework adapter sends only changed elements as atomic mutation batches. Animations run natively in Rust (no per-frame React render). Ships bunx @gpuix/cli new, standalone binaries via bun build --compile + cargo-packager, and an automation API that can click/screenshot a window without stealing your focus (focus: false). ~2.6k★.

github.com/remorses/gpuix

Zele
Multi-account email & calendar CLI — Gmail, Outlook/Microsoft (XOAUTH2), IMAP/SMTP (Fastmail, Proton Bridge, anything), plus free receive-only @zele.sh inboxes (up to 10). SQLite cache, YAML output for piping through yq. Read/search/send/reply/forward, drafts, labels, filters, attachments, Google Calendar, mail watch to block until a matching email arrives. Built for agents: zele --help is the source of truth, never use the TUI, run zele whoami before --account, reply refuses to send on a stale view. Interactive TUI needs Bun; CLI works on Node ≥22.16.
npm install -g zele
zele mail list --filter "is:unread" --limit 100 | yq '.[].id' | xargs zele mail read

web-fetch-by-client.title: Web fetch by client
web-fetch-by-client.content:
Web fetch by client
Which URL-fetch / web-fetch tools each model will actually accept. Learned the hard way.

































Client.html.txt.jsonNotesGemini✅❌❌Non-HTML fails with URL_FETCH_STATUS_MISC_ERROR. A plain .txt and a .json both failed; the root HTML URL went through immediately. Its fetcher only accepts text/html.ChatGPT✅✅✅Corrected 2026-10-16 — the original claim was WRONG. ChatGPT read /static/contentIndex.json (note bodies and all), the light JSON, and the plain-text index. Not restricted to HTML. However, its flaky.DeepSeek✅✅✅Accepts all three. No format restriction observed.
Correction (2026-10-16)
ChatGPT can read .json and .txt. An earlier version of this note said otherwise — that claim was
wrong and is retracted. Only Gemini has shown a format restriction. Treat per-client format support
as volatile: publish all three formats, and test rather than assume.
The full index is the rich one
static/contentIndex.json carries each note’s title, filePath, links, tags, and full
content — i.e. the whole vault in one fetch. The light JSON is the same minus bodies, for
cheap navigation. If a client can read JSON at all, this is the one to give it.
The practical consequence
Never expose one artifact format. Whatever you want an agent to read, publish it in three shapes:

.html — for HTML-only fetchers (Gemini, ChatGPT)
.json — for JSON-only / structured clients
.txt — for text/plain-only fetchers

That’s exactly why this vault’s map exists three times, with the same content. Live, on the published vault:

unixuserdev.github.io/obsidian-vault/llms.html
unixuserdev.github.io/obsidian-vault/llms.json
unixuserdev.github.io/obsidian-vault/llms.txt

Diagnosis trick: if a fetch fails, try the HTML version of the same thing. If HTML works, it’s a content-type restriction, not a network block.

memory/appimage-leaks-ld_library_path-an.title: AppImage leaks LD_LIBRARY_PATH and breaks notify-send
memory/appimage-leaks-ld_library_path-an.content:
The OpenCode AppImage on this CachyOS box exports LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/tmp/.mount_OpenCo*/usr/lib into every child process of the agent session. System binaries then load the AppImage’s bundled libraries instead of the system ones — notify-send dies with “symbol lookup error: notify-send: undefined symbol: notify_notification_get_activation_app_launch_context” because the AppImage ships an older libnotify.so.4. Fix: strip LD_LIBRARY_PATH/LD_PRELOAD from the child environment (env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH, or subprocess env=). The systemd —user environment is NOT polluted, so timer- and service-launched processes are unaffected. Check with systemctl --user show-environment.

memory/brick-rigs-minimize-crash-fixed-b.title: Brick Rigs minimize crash fixed by running it in gamescope
memory/brick-rigs-minimize-crash-fixed-b.content:
Brick Rigs (Steam appid 552100, native UE4.27 Linux Vulkan build) crashed every time its window was minimized on this machine. Root cause: the game runs as an X11 client under Xwayland (KDE Plasma 6.8 Wayland session, NVIDIA open driver 615.78.08, RTX 4060). Unmapping the X11 window wedges UE4’s Vulkan present path; the NVIDIA driver’s watchdog fires NVRM: Xid 109 (CTX SWITCH TIMEOUT) and kills the context, giving VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST and a GPUCrash dump (6 identical dumps in ~/.config/Epic/BrickRigs/SavedRemastered/Crashes). Windowed, borderless-fullscreen and resized windows all crashed identically, so no in-game setting fixes it.
Fix applied: installed gamescope and set the Steam launch option to gamescope -W 1920 -H 1080 -r 120 -f -- %command%. Verified: launched through Steam, minimized and restored the gamescope window via a KWin script — game survived, zero Xid 109, no new crash dump, still rendering at 60% GPU util. Undo by clearing the launch option in Steam properties.

memory/feynman's-restaurant-problem-and-.title: Feynman's restaurant problem and how people actually decide
memory/feynman's-restaurant-problem-and-.content:
Feynman’s “restaurant problem” (posed on a napkin, unpublished, died 1988) asks: over N nights, when do you try a new restaurant vs. return to the best one you’ve found? You can go back, so it’s an explore/exploit + optimal stopping problem.
Feynman’s answer: a moving bar that starts high and decays. Early on, keep exploring unless you hit something exceptional, because you still have many nights to revisit a great find. Each passing night makes exploration worth less, so near the end even a “merely good” place is good enough.
A 2026 study (Griffiths et al., Princeton) proved Feynman’s math correct and tested real people: 2,520 participants, virtual city, 7/14/28 nights to maximize total score, four quality distributions (uniform, exponential, power law, triangular).

People did NOT follow Feynman’s exact curve.
They used a simpler rule: start with a high standard, then lower it in a straight line over the trip. They also explored more than optimal early.
That shortcut still captured ~90% of the value of the optimal strategy.
Participants adapted: higher starting bar when rare gems were plausible, settled sooner when options were clustered.

Lesson: fast “good enough” heuristics (resource rationality) get near-optimal results without the perfect calculation. Relevant to modeling human behavior in AI systems.
Source: ZME Science / The Guardian coverage of the 2026 study, Jun 2026.

memory/larping-another-distro-in-fastfet.title: Larping another distro in fastfetch
memory/larping-another-distro-in-fastfet.content:
On the CachyOS box, fastfetch (2.70) can be made to display any other distro. There is no runtime override for the OS detection — paths are compile-time macros, no —target-dir flag. Three ways: (1) fastfetch --logo <name> changes only the ASCII (544 built-ins via —list-logos; the OS line still says CachyOS). (2) A JSON config with "logo": {"source": "..."} plus custom modules for faked key/values — note custom/command modules cannot be used via -s/—structure, only in JSON. A working one lives at /OpenCode-Sandbox/Temp/larp.jsonc. (3) Full unprivileged spoof: fake an os-release file and bind-mount it with bwrap — bwrap --dev-bind / / --ro-bind Temp/fake-os-release /etc/os-release -- fastfetch -s title:os:logo — which auto-picks the logo and rewrites the OS line. Gotchas: Ubuntu flavour detection reads XDG_CONFIG_DIRS (KDE -> reports Kubuntu; set —setenv XDG_CONFIG_DIRS /etc/xdg for plain Ubuntu); the hostname still leaks via the title module; a fake ID=windows auto-picks the legacy tilted-flag logo, not the flat “Windows 11” one.

memory/roblox-studio-mcp-bridge-on-linux.title: Roblox Studio MCP bridge on Linux via Vinegar
memory/roblox-studio-mcp-bridge-on-linux.content:
Roblox Studio’s MCP server (StudioMCP.exe, “studio_mcp_proxy”) now works on Linux. The wrapper is /OpenCode-Sandbox/roblox-studio-mcp/roblox-studio-mcp.sh (registered in OpenCode as the local MCP server “roblox-studio”). KEY FIX: do NOT run the proxy under Vinegar’s bundled patched Wine (“kombucha”) — its socket layer never delivers readiness to tokio, so the proxy binds 127.0.0.1:13469 but never accepts a connection, tools/list stays empty, and Studio’s main thread hangs (StudioHangMonitor) which wedges the wineserver. Run StudioMCP.exe with STOCK SYSTEM WINE in its own prefix (~/.wine-studiomcp) instead, with /drive_c/users//AppData/Local/Roblox symlinked to Vinegar’s appdata/Roblox so it shares auth.token and ClientSettings. Studio<->proxy is pure TCP loopback, so no shared Wine prefix is needed. Verified: Studio connects and the MCP client receives 28 tools; Studio survives proxy disconnects without hanging.

memory/tiny-core-logo-merged-into-fastfe.title: Tiny Core logo merged into fastfetch
memory/tiny-core-logo-merged-into-fastfe.content:

PR fastfetch-cli/fastfetch#2655 “Logo (Builtin): add Tiny Core Linux” landed on 2026-10-16 (merge commit 99785f54, merged by maintainer CarterLi), closing issue #2654. src/logo/ascii/t/tinycore.txt is live on dev and ships with the next release. Filed under the UnixUserDev account (fork UnixUserDev/fastfetch, branch logo/tinycore, base dev).
The logo is the project’s own mark: a 21x10 sphere split diagonally, “tiny” upper-left / “micro” lower-right — the “o” of core. $1 = FF_COLOR_FG_BLUE (matching the distro’s own ANSI_COLOR="0;34"), $2 = FF_COLOR_FG_LIGHT_WHITE. Registered in src/logo/ascii/t.inc between TileOS and Torizon OS.
The single review comment was “Only one entry is allowed here. The ID TinyCore (case insensitive) should only be used” — fixed by reducing the names array to one entry, { "TinyCore" }. Matching is case-insensitive, so one name already covers both ID=tinycore and NAME=TinyCore; invented aliases are not wanted.
Upstream process for logos, learned the hard way:

A Logo Request issue must exist before the PR, and the PR body must say Closes #N. Logo PRs without one are rejected by their template.
The art must be under 50x20, use $N colour placeholders only, and carry no trailing spaces.
You cannot set labels on a repository where you lack write access.

Motive: fastfetch shipped 544 built-in logos but none for Tiny Core, so it drew generic Tux. Tiny Core ranks #113 in DistroWatch’s page-hit ranking — above roughly 104 distros that already have artwork.

memory/verified-bubblewrap-sandbox-recip.content:
For the BYOA harness sandbox (bubblewrap 0.13.1 at /usr/bin/bwrap, unprivileged userns enabled, uid 1000) these recipes were executed and verified:
Base: bwrap —ro-bind / / —dev /dev —proc /proc —tmpfs /tmp —bind “WORK" "WORK” —chdir “WORK" --die-with-parent --new-session --setenv HOME "WORK” /bin/sh -c ’…’
Gotchas found by testing, not docs:

With —ro-bind / /, any bind whose DESTINATION does not exist fails hard: “bwrap: Can’t create file /mnt/extra: Read-only file system” — and —dir does NOT fix it. Fixes that work: put —tmpfs on the parent first (—tmpfs /mnt then —ro-bind SRC /mnt/extra), pre-create the dir on the host, or skip —ro-bind / / and build a skeleton root (/usr /etc /bin /lib /lib64 + —dir /opt).
—unshare-all gives a netns where lo is ALREADY up with 127.0.0.1/8, so local bind/connect works and outbound is dead. Do not try “ip link set lo up” — it fails with RTNETLINK Operation not permitted even at uid 0 inside the userns.
—unshare-all —share-net exposes the HOST netns (reaches host 127.0.0.1 but also LAN/internet). There is no “host loopback only” flag. To reach exactly one service, keep —unshare-all and bind only that service’s unix socket directory — AF_UNIX works across net isolation.
Missing —proc /proc breaks tools that read /proc/self/*. Missing /etc/resolv.conf breaks DNS only when /etc is shadowed; re-bind resolv.conf + hosts to restore.
uid mapping: —unshare-all alone still shows uid=1000; —unshare-user —uid 0 —gid 0 gives uid=0 inside.

memory/byoa/byoa-v0.2.0-release-status.title: BYOA v0.2.0 release status
memory/byoa/byoa-v0.2.0-release-status.content:
Version: 0.2.0
Release tag: v0.2.0
Repository: github.com/UnixUserDev/byoa
Releases: github.com/UnixUserDev/byoa/releases
License: MIT
BYOA stands for Bring Your Own Agent: a local-first, bring-your-own-agent coding harness, released publicly on GitHub.
Included: the core agent loop, OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic providers (plus local servers such as LM Studio, Ollama and llama.cpp), session persistence with resume, the shell and file tools, the bubblewrap sandbox with a read-allowlist skeleton root, three prompt tiers (lite/normal/large), namespaced Obsidian-backed memory, and a TUI (—tui) on OpenTUI.
Not included yet: Web and Electron adapters, MCP, subagents, and web fetch/search.
Distribution: releases ship built artifacts (standalone tarball with node_modules beside the launcher, and an npm-installable tarball). The source tree is not an installable package because Node cannot type-strip TypeScript inside node_modules.
Quality: 212 tests passing including real-bubblewrap isolation tests and headless OpenTUI render tests; tsc —noEmit clean. Requires Node 26 or newer; bubblewrap is needed for sandboxing, and strict mode (the default) refuses to run unwrapped when it is missing.
